title: Pāhi no agna enase: four offerings for protection
theme: Four short offering verses asking Agni to protect the worshipper, the worshipper’s knowledge, the rite and everything.

words.context: Anonymous: «नोऽस्मानेनसो ज्ञानप्रतिबन्धकात्पापात्पाहि» — protect us from sin that blocks knowledge

words.gram: n. dat. sg. (in the sense of the ablative)
words.context: Bhāskara: «एनसे एनसः । विभक्तिव्यत्ययः» — enase for enasaḥ, a change of case
Anonymous: «विश्वेवेदसे कृत्स्नतत्त्वज्ञानसिद्धार्थ» — for attaining knowledge of the whole truth
Anonymous: «विशेषेण भानं दीप्तिर्विभा सैव वसु धनं यस्याग्नेः सोऽयं विभावसुः»
Anonymous: «सर्वं ज्ञानसाधनं गुरुशास्त्रादिकं» — every means to knowledge, the teacher, the scripture and the rest

words.meaning: O you of a hundred rites
words.context: Anonymous: «शतसंख्याः क्रतवो येनाग्निना निष्पाद्यन्ते सोऽयं शतक्रतुः»

sandhi.type: e before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: -e becomes -ay before a vowel and the y is dropped, leaving a gap: agna enase.

sandhi_exceptions.note: no · agne: the a of agne is not elided after no, as often in Vedic recitation (classical no ’gne); every witness prints the two words apart.

samasa.meaning: all knowledge; one who knows all

morphology.note: Vedic: before a, naḥ is written no and the a of agne is not elided (classical no ’gne); the record declares the gap as a sandhi exception.
Dative. The anonymous commentator reads it as the purpose, ‘for complete knowledge’; Bhāskara as an epithet of the god, ‘to you who know all’ («विश्ववेदसे विश्वस्य वेदित्रे»).

translation.literal: Protect us, O Agni, from sin — svāhā. Protect us for [our] complete knowledge — svāhā. Protect the sacrifice, O rich in radiance — svāhā. Protect everything, O you of a hundred rites — svāhā.
translation.readable: Agni, guard us from wrongdoing; guard us so that we may know fully; radiant one, guard the rite; lord of a hundred rites, guard everything. Svāhā at each.

syntax: Four parallel imperative clauses, each pāhi with an object (implied ‘us’, yajñam, sarvam) and a vocative or dative, each closed by svāhā.

ambiguities.note: A purpose (‘for complete knowledge’, the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa) or an epithet of the god (‘to you who know all’, Bhāskara).

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Bhāskara calls it an anuṣṭubh whose four pādas each end in svāhā («स्वाहाकारान्तपादचतुष्टया अनुष्टुबेषा»). With svāhā each printed line counts 10 syllables (8 + 2).

beginner: Four very short offerings, each ending with svāhā, the word spoken as something is placed in a sacred fire. Each asks Agni, the fire, to protect: first “us” from wrongdoing, then us for the sake of full knowledge, then the rite itself, and finally everything. The god is addressed by two old titles, “rich in radiance” and “lord of a hundred rites”. The commentators say these offerings belong to someone seeking liberation: they ask that whatever stands in the way of knowledge be removed, and that the teacher, the scriptures and the other means to knowledge be kept safe. Bhāskara says that from here on the anuvākas are for meditation. The record reports these readings and claims nothing about what the offering achieves.
analogy: Like asking a guard to keep the traveller, the road, the luggage and then simply everything safe.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Four offerings with svāhā ask Agni to protect us from sin, to protect us for complete knowledge, to protect the sacrifice and to protect everything.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: these are homa mantras for one seeking release, to obtain knowledge by removing its obstacles — «अथ प्रतिबन्धनिवारणेन मुमुक्षोर्ज्ञानप्राप्त्यर्थं होममन्त्रा उच्यन्ते» (anonymous). The sin to be guarded against is what obstructs knowledge («ज्ञानप्रतिबन्धकात्पापात्»), and ‘everything’ is the means to knowledge: the teacher, scripture and the rest.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara says the anuvākas from here are for meditation («इत उत्तरे अनुवाका उपासनार्थाः»). He takes the sacrifice as one made of knowledge («नो ऽस्मदीयं यज्ञं ज्ञानात्मकं पाहि») and explains enase as a change of case, from sin.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: No differences are listed for this anuvāka. The printed नो अग्न keeps the a unelided, a common Vedic spelling; see the sandhi exception.

schools.disagreement: The commentaries available are ritual and Vedic; none takes a Vedānta-school position. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here).

contemporary.text: The prayer asks protection not only for the learner but for the rite, the teacher and the books — the conditions under which learning happens. Looking after those conditions is part of learning anything well. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: The prayer moves from “us” to “the rite” to “everything”. Why that order?
reflect.deeper: Is “knowledge” here the goal of the rite (the anonymous commentator) or the nature of the rite itself (Bhāskara’s “sacrifice made of knowledge”)?
reflect.practice: Name one condition your own learning depends on, and do one thing to protect it.
